author: andrewljohnson
cardQuote: I'm usually pretty optimistic on new YC start-ups, but I'm not sure the world needs another uptime monitor. There are so many free, cheap, and other services like this that it's hard to imagine what a company might differentiate on to become the "next big thing."
quote: I'm usually pretty optimistic on new YC start-ups, but I'm not sure the world needs another uptime monitor. There are so many free, cheap, and other services like this that it's hard to imagine what a company might differentiate on to become the "next big thing."
storyTitle: PagerDuty (YC S10) Makes Sure Your Team Knows When A Server Goes Down
outcome: IPO on the NYSE in 2019; still a leading incident-management platform.
outcomeDetail: PagerDuty went public in April 2019 and built a business around on-call scheduling, escalation, and incident response. It remains one of the default tools for engineering operations.
note: The critique assumed "uptime monitor" was the category. PagerDuty sold the human workflow around alerts—who gets woken up, when, and how it escalates—and that turned out to be a durable enterprise need.

author: nivertech
cardQuote: Twilio always seems like a hack to me. Once VoiceXML/CCML was hot market with many startups competing, with biggest exit being Tellme acquired by Microsoft for $800M (same people who founded Zappos).
quote: Twilio always seems like a hack to me. Once VoiceXML/CCML was hot market with many startups competing, with biggest exit being Tellme acquired by Microsoft for $800M (same people who founded Zappos). So what's new Twilio can offer here? I have no idea why USV invested in them...
storyTitle: Why choose Tropo over Twilio
outcome: IPO in 2016; annual revenue passed $4B in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Twilio turned programmable voice and SMS into a public company, then added SendGrid and Segment. Revenue reached $4.15B in 2023, and the company remains a core communications API for developers.
note: The "hack" was the product: Twilio hid telecom plumbing behind a clean HTTP API. VoiceXML's prior failure didn't preclude a developer-first platform from winning.

author: staunch
cardQuote: Sending email isn't hard. Amazon SES solved that. Receiving email is just slightly more work, but still well within the comfort zone of most developers
quote: Twilio is awesome because setting up Asterisk and acquiring phone numbers is a big pain in the butt and requires knowledge most web developers don't have. Sending email isn't hard. Amazon SES solved that. Receiving email is just slightly more work, but still well within the comfort zone of most developers: $ cat /etc/aliases comment_reply: "|/path/to/email_handler"
storyTitle: Mailgun (YC W11) Raises $1.1 Million For Its "Twilio For Email"
outcome: Acquired by Sinch for about $1.9B in 2021.
outcomeDetail: Mailgun became a core transactional-email API, was acquired by Rackspace, spun back out as part of Pathwire, and was sold to Sinch in a deal valued at roughly $1.9B. It still processes billions of emails for developers.
note: Staunch was right that sending email is easy; he underestimated deliverability, inbound parsing, and the operational mess that developers would pay to avoid.

author: ChuckChuck
cardQuote: SendGrid has about 1 month to lower it's price to at least $0.20 per thousand if they want to keep my company (We send about 3 million emails per month).
quote: SendGrid has about 1 month to lower it's price to at least $0.20 per thousand if they want to keep my company (We send about 3 million emails per month). They have provided me with a good service so far and I hope they are ready to compete on price.
storyTitle: SendGrid Responds to Amazon's Simple Email Service
outcome: IPO in 2017; acquired by Twilio for about $3B in 2019.
outcomeDetail: SendGrid went public in November 2017 and was bought by Twilio in an all-stock deal valued at roughly $3B. It became the email arm of Twilio's customer-engagement platform.
note: The price pressure from Amazon SES was real, but SendGrid competed on deliverability and tooling rather than matching SES per-message. The one-month ultimatum didn't sink it.

author: dreamdu5t
cardQuote: Asana is yet another tasklist. Trello is an innovation. I get the feeling that Asana is built for the people who built it, whereas Trello was built for everyone.
quote: Asana is yet another tasklist. Trello is an innovation. I get the feeling that Asana is built for the people who built it, whereas Trello was built for everyone. Despite this, Asana should be praised for utilizing keyboard shortcuts. I see no feature beyond the basic tasklist features that all PM software has. Not even velocity like Pivotal Tracker. What is innovative about Asana? The customer doesn't give a shit whether it's done in Luna.
storyTitle: Introducing Asana: The Modern Way to Work Together
outcome: Direct-listed in 2020; revenue passed $650M in fiscal 2024.
outcomeDetail: Asana grew from a task list into a work-management platform and went public via a direct listing in September 2020. It reported $652.5M in revenue for fiscal 2024 and still counts large enterprises among its customers.
note: The "yet another tasklist" read missed the coordination layer Asana was building. Trello won the kanban aesthetic, but Asana won budgets for cross-team planning.

author: cletus
cardQuote: At the risk of being negative, can I just say that for me, as a consumer or customer, when companies start offering lifetime deals for a one-time fee, it's a huge red flag.
quote: At the risk of being negative, can I just say that for me, as a consumer or customer, when companies start offering lifetime deals for a one-time fee, it's a huge red flag. Why? Because often it's a desperate move done by a company to generate cash flow. It's not ultimately sustainable either. Theoretically you could be providing that same service 10+ years down the track. You might (reasonably) assume some attrition in the time but you get my point. Too many times I've seen this done as a company's last move before filing for bankruptcy. Disclaimer: I'm speaking generally here. I know nothing of Mixpanel's circumstances (financial or otherwise) and certainly don't mean to impugn them, their management team, their founders or their employees. Providing a free service is different. Typically this is done as a "freemium" model where you hope a certain percentage of free users will later convert to paying users. People know this and have a different level of expectation than for something they've paid for, even if that something is a nominal one-off fee (you and they may also disagree about what constitutes "nominal"). As a paid service, due to consumer protection, etc you may have to meet a higher standard but IANAL.
storyTitle: Lifetime Mixpanel.com Startup Plan - $17
outcome: Valued at $1.05B in 2021; still independent.
outcomeDetail: Mixpanel survived the lifetime-deal era, refocused on product analytics, and raised a $200M Series C at a $1.05B valuation in 2021. It remains an independent company with thousands of paying customers.
note: Cletus explicitly said he was speaking generally, and the lifetime deal was a customer-acquisition stunt, not a last resort. Mixpanel kept the free tier and turned it into a real business.

author: troels
cardQuote: Actually - and I'm not just trying to be snarky here - but I don't get what you offer, that ifttt don't? Perhaps except the presentation is a bit more inclusive. Is that it?
quote: Actually - and I'm not just trying to be snarky here - but I don't get what you offer, that ifttt don't? Perhaps except the presentation is a bit more inclusive. Is that it?
storyTitle: Zapier (YC S12): An IFTTT For Business Users
outcome: Valued at $5B in 2021 after raising only about $1.3M.
outcomeDetail: Zapier became the default no-code automation layer between SaaS apps, reaching a $5B valuation in 2021 after raising only about $1.3M. It remained independent and expanded to thousands of integrations.
note: The IFTTT comparison was fair on the surface, but Zapier targeted business users and long-tail app integrations. That unglamorous catalog became the moat.

author: bittersweet
cardQuote: On first glance it would seem it offers exactly the same functionality with the added benefit of your errors already going to an external location.
quote: I'm not a Django user myself, but why use a solution like this over let's say Hoptoad via http://sjl.bitbucket.org/django-hoptoad/ ? On first glance it would seem it offers exactly the same functionality with the added benefit of your errors already going to an external location.
storyTitle: Sentry, Disqus' near realtime logging app for Django
outcome: Valued at $3B in 2022; used by tens of thousands of organizations.
outcomeDetail: Sentry grew from a Disqus side project into an open-source error-tracking standard, adding performance monitoring and session replay. It raised $90M at a $3B valuation in 2022.
note: Hoptoad was the incumbent, but Sentry's open-source core and developer-first workflow let it become the default. "Same functionality" missed the distribution advantage.

author: CameronBanga
cardQuote: Was excited after visiting that landing page, but woof on the pricing. We do custom app development for a variety of large companies, so do hear "analytics, analytics, analytics" all the time. But I would just hear "go with Google Analytics" at those prices.
quote: Was excited after visiting that landing page, but woof on the pricing. We do custom app development for a variety of large companies, so do hear "analytics, analytics, analytics" all the time. But I would just hear "go with Google Analytics" at those prices.
storyTitle: Mobile Analytics Platform Amplitude (YC W12) Takes On Flurry and Mixpanel
outcome: Direct-listed in 2021; revenue passed $275M in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Amplitude went public via direct listing in September 2021 at a $7.1B first-day valuation. It reported $276.3M in revenue for 2023 and continues to sell product analytics to enterprises.
note: The pricing objection was real—Amplitude was never cheap—but "go with Google Analytics" underestimated how much teams would pay for event-level product analytics.

author: mlhamel
cardQuote: I'm a bit confused. The more i read the doc, the more i feel it look Just Another Queue system. I don't really see the difference between Kafka and let's say RabbitMQ, Celery or also statsd...
quote: I'm a bit confused. The more i read the doc, the more i feel it look Just Another Queue system. I don't really see the difference between Kafka and let's say RabbitMQ, Celery or also statsd...
storyTitle: Confluent, a company for Apache Kafka and realtime data
outcome: IPO in 2021; IBM acquired it for $11B in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Confluent commercialized Kafka and built a cloud data-streaming business, going public in 2021. IBM announced an $11B acquisition in December 2025 and completed it in March 2026.
note: Kafka looked like "just another queue" if you only compared message delivery. Confluent sold replayable logs, connectors, schema management, and streaming infrastructure—a different category.

author: flavio81
cardQuote: Really? I thought the MongoDB fad had gone away, that common sense returned, and people either used proper document stores, or proper relational databases, or graph databases.
quote: Really? I thought the MongoDB fad had gone away, that common sense returned, and people either used proper document stores, or proper relational databases, or graph databases.
storyTitle: MongoDB has filed confidentially for IPO
outcome: IPO in 2017; revenue passed $1.6B in fiscal 2024.
outcomeDetail: MongoDB went public in October 2017 and grew into a multi-billion-dollar database company, with Atlas becoming the majority of its revenue. Fiscal 2024 revenue was $1.68B.
note: The "fad" call came at the IPO, after a decade of production use. MongoDB's document model found a durable niche, especially for developer-facing apps and Atlas.

storyTitle: Cisco Is Said to Have Offered $7B-Plus for DataDog
outcome: IPO in 2019; revenue passed $2B in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Datadog went public in September 2019 and became one of the largest observability companies, with $2.13B in 2023 revenue and a place in the S&P 500. The predicted race to the bottom didn't happen.
note: The competitor list was real, but Datadog's integrations, dashboards, and developer experience let it consolidate spend rather than compete on price alone.

author: tekkk
cardQuote: This is some ridiculous overvaluation. I've used their product and while it worked all right, I could definitely notice part of their websites and docs being half-assed by not very experienced web developers.
quote: This is some ridiculous overvaluation. I've used their product and while it worked all right, I could definitely notice part of their websites and docs being half-assed by not very experienced web developers. Which didn't really conjure an impression of quality to me. More like, "let's do things in hurry to get the money". I don't know how can you, as an investor, rationalize the price by any other reason than speculative increase in share price. Which is again driven by some fundamentals but mostly by hype. If they fail to gain almost 100% increase in revenue for the next year, that 60B is looking way too high. Compare this with something like Splunk. They make high quality product and have over 2B in revenue (with a nice growth curve). Market cap 30B. So is Snowflake as of now worth two Splunks? I don't think so. I could see it maybe being half of that, 15B, if I squint real hard.
storyTitle: Why is Snowflake so Valuable?
outcome: IPO in 2020; revenue passed $2.8B in fiscal 2024.
outcomeDetail: Snowflake's September 2020 IPO was the largest software IPO to date, and the company kept growing, reporting $2.8B in fiscal 2024 revenue. It did not collapse to the $15B valuation the comment suggested.
note: The UI/docs critique may have been fair, but it confused a rushed website with the product. Snowflake's separation of storage and compute was the real story.

author: its_a_random_ac
cardQuote: Yeah, I'd like to know too, from everything I can see it's just a cloud-hosted notebook with a spark backend, which does have some benefits, but I can't tell why they got as big as they did.
quote: Yeah, I'd like to know too, from everything I can see it's just a cloud-hosted notebook with a spark backend, which does have some benefits, but I can't tell why they got as big as they did. Also from a more cynical side, I've interviewed at a lot of companies that ask if I've used it before, and I'm really temped to just lie, since it feels like something that could be picked up really easily.
storyTitle: Most companies do not need Snowflake or Databricks
outcome: Valued at over $100B in 2025; revenue run-rate passed $4B.
outcomeDetail: Databricks turned Spark and lakehouse tooling into a cloud data and AI platform. It raised a Series K at a valuation above $100B in 2025 and crossed a $4B revenue run-rate.
note: The "cloud-hosted notebook" view missed the platform underneath: managed Spark, Delta Lake, governance, and later AI tooling. The valuation did not stay at the level the comment implied.

author: bastardoperator
cardQuote: I've never wanted a company or people to fail but the amount of misery this product has brought coworkers and myself, I'm shocked it's in a position to file for IPO.
quote: This is one of the worst tools I've ever used and we tried hard for a year. Besides the interface being clunky and slow it lets you delete important things on accident with multiple people in our group having fallen victim to it's non intuitive UI. I've never wanted a company or people to fail but the amount of misery this product has brought coworkers and myself, I'm shocked it's in a position to file for IPO.
storyTitle: Monday.com Files IPO
outcome: IPO in 2021; revenue passed $700M in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Monday.com went public in June 2021 and kept growing, reporting $729.7M in 2023 revenue and more than $1B in 2025. Whatever the usability complaints, the company found a large paying market.
note: The product critique was specific and may reflect real pain, but it treated one team's bad experience as a verdict on the whole company. Monday's growth came from less technical buyers the commenter wasn't accounting for.

author: zdrummond
cardQuote: How and why should I trust a brand-new startup? Doubly so when they don't even list security in their docs.
quote: I wish things like this would start of as an open-source and/or stand-alone app. It looks great, and I want to play with it. But Excel is at it's core used for very sensitive data. Financials, budgets, customer lists, biz plans, etc. How and why should I trust a brand-new startup? Doubly so when they don't even list security in their docs. tl;dr; I love the idea, looks like a great implementation, please let me demo (and then ideally purchase) an on-prem version.
storyTitle: Show HN: Retool: Excel-like, with higher order primitives
outcome: Valued at $3.2B in 2022; used by thousands of companies.
outcomeDetail: Retool became the default internal-tool builder for engineering teams and raised $45M at a $3.2B valuation in 2022. It also suffered a major 2023 security incident that made the trust question look prescient.
note: The security concern was legitimate—Retool had a serious breach in 2023—but it didn't stop adoption. The comment was right about the risk and wrong about the ceiling.

author: slotrans
cardQuote: AWS Secrets Manager gives me everything I want, for no effort, and costs rounds-down-to-zero. I cannot begin to imagine what Vault could even offer that would tempt me to switch.
quote: AWS Secrets Manager gives me everything I want, for no effort, and costs rounds-down-to-zero. I cannot begin to imagine what Vault could even offer that would tempt me to switch.
storyTitle: HashiCorp – S1
outcome: IPO in 2021; IBM acquired it for $6.4B in 2025.
outcomeDetail: HashiCorp built Terraform, Vault, Consul, and Nomad into core infrastructure tooling, went public in 2021, and was acquired by IBM for $6.4B. Vault alone became a standard for secrets management.
note: AWS Secrets Manager covered the simple case, but Vault sold dynamic credentials, auditability, and multi-cloud policy. The comment mistook a narrow use case for the whole market.

author: kirillzubovsky
cardQuote: Well, to answer your question, they have all the funding but no ability to innovate, so like every other large company, they chose to copy what already works.
quote: Well, to answer your question, they have all the funding but no ability to innovate, so like every other large company, they chose to copy what already works. Their money is better spent on getting big clients with deep pockets, then to worry about UX. Clearly, this is not a good reason on your end, but they can, so they do.
storyTitle: DocuSign, with $230M in funding, why are you copying HelloSign?
outcome: IPO in 2018; revenue passed $2.7B in fiscal 2024.
outcomeDetail: DocuSign went public in April 2018 and kept expanding from e-signatures into contract lifecycle management. It reported $2.76B in revenue for fiscal 2024.
note: The copying critique was fair—DocuSign did lift HelloSign's onboarding—but it was a category leader defending share, not a company out of ideas. The innovation criticism didn't translate into commercial failure.

storyTitle: HubSpot files for $100M IPO
outcome: IPO in 2014; revenue passed $2B in 2023.
outcomeDetail: HubSpot went public in October 2014 and compounded into a multi-billion-dollar CRM and marketing platform. It reported $2.17B in 2023 revenue and more than 200,000 customers.
note: The bubble call was wrong about the company, though it was right that public markets were paying up for growth. HubSpot's subscription revenue and customer base kept expanding long after the IPO.

author: trustfundbaby
cardQuote: New Relic needs competition not funding. Their prices are ridiculous and there's nobody to keep them honest because they're the only game in town.
quote: New Relic needs competition not funding. Their prices are ridiculous and there's nobody to keep them honest because they're the only game in town.
storyTitle: Why New Relic Is Raising $80 Million Now
outcome: IPO in 2014; taken private for $6.5B in 2023.
outcomeDetail: New Relic went public in December 2014 and became a standard APM tool, though Datadog and cloud-native rivals eroded its position. Francisco Partners and TPG acquired it for $6.5B in 2023.
note: The pricing complaint was prescient—competition did arrive and New Relic lost share—but "only game in town" underestimated the market. The company still exited at $6.5B.
